evals.prompt: We're Formline, a form-analytics SaaS (free plan up to 500 submissions/month, Pro is $29/mo). Our WordPress plugin has a Settings tab, a free Insights tab, and a Pro tab with A/B testing and heatmaps that's visible but greyed out with an 'Upgrade' button until the site enters a Pro license key. We also want a 14-day Pro trial that switches itself off inside the plugin. Can you check this setup and get it ready to submit to WordPress.org next week?
evals.expected_output: Flags the greyed-out Pro tab and in-plugin 14-day trial as trialware, moves paid enforcement to the Formline service (plan and quota returned by the API) or an off-directory add-on, ranks those options, and lists the readme/service disclosure work before submitting.
expectations: Identifies the locked, greyed-out Pro tab behind a license key as trialware banned by the directory guidelines
Identifies the 14-day trial that disables itself inside the plugin as banned (functionality disabled after a trial period)
Recommends enforcing the Pro plan in the Formline service (API returns plan or quota limits) rather than in plugin code
Offers a separate premium add-on sold and hosted outside WordPress.org as the alternative for features that must run locally
Ranks the paid-value options with service-side enforcement as the default for a SaaS
Tells the user to remove Pro-only code and named Pro feature stubs from the directory plugin, not just hide them
States that the free plugin may link to the paid offer but must not install the add-on or premium code itself
Limits upgrade prompts to the plugin's own settings page or contextual spots, with any site-wide notice dismissible
Requires an External services section in the readme naming the Formline API, data sent, when, and terms and privacy links
Notes the 500-submission free quota is acceptable only when the service enforces it, not a local counter in the plugin
Does not propose a license-key validation endpoint as the 'service' that unlocks local code

evals.prompt: I run a small agency. Our client Brevlo (email marketing SaaS) wants an official 'Brevlo Forms' plugin live on WordPress.org before their customer conference on the 14th, which is 10 days away. I'll submit it from my personal wordpress.org account (my gmail) since I'm the dev, and we'll hand it to them later. We have a second plugin for another client ready too, so I'll submit both today. Brevlo's website for the plugin is still a coming-soon page. What's the plan?
evals.expected_output: Moves submission to Brevlo's own company account with a company-domain email, explains the brand-first slug and its permanence, one-submission-at-a-time, live website requirement, no queue jumping, and a launch plan that survives approval missing the conference.
expectations: Says the official Brevlo plugin must be submitted from Brevlo's own WordPress.org account with a company-domain email, not the agency's personal gmail account
Explains that a slug or name starting with the Brevlo brand is reserved to the brand owner and gets flagged when a non-owner submits
States the slug is permanent once the plugin is approved
Mentions the slug can be checked in the confirmation email and changed only once before approval
States only one plugin can be in review per account at a time, so both plugins cannot be submitted together from one account
Warns against creating extra accounts to get around the one-at-a-time limit
Requires the plugin and author URLs plus terms and privacy pages to be live before submitting, so the coming-soon page must be finished first
States there is no queue jumping for a launch date (only security or legal issues)
Gives a launch fallback such as announcing the plugin as coming to WordPress.org if approval misses the conference
Requires 2FA on the submitting and committer accounts
Marks review-time figures as variable or to verify rather than promising a fixed approval date
Says to reply to the review email to fix a wrong submitting account rather than resubmitting

evals.prompt: Our product team specced the v1 WordPress connector for Tallyhub (customer support SaaS): 1) the admin page is an iframe of app.tallyhub.io so we don't rebuild the dashboard, 2) the chat widget JS and our admin UI library load from our CDN so we can hotfix without releases, 3) on activation we POST the site URL and admin email to our API for install analytics, 4) a 'Get Tallyhub Pro' button that downloads and installs our pro add-on zip from our servers, 5) 'Powered by Tallyhub' in the site footer, on by default, 6) the readme headline says 'Makes your support desk 100% GDPR compliant'. Anything we need to change before submitting?
evals.expected_output: Flags all six items with the fix for each: local settings screen calling the API, bundled admin assets (service widget acceptable only as the service, documented), no activation call before consent, no installing off-directory code, credit off by default, 'helps' compliance wording.
expectations: Flags the iframed admin page as banned and recommends building the admin screen locally and calling the Tallyhub API
Flags loading admin UI JavaScript or CSS from a CDN as banned and requires shipping it inside the plugin
Distinguishes the customer-facing chat widget served by the service itself as a possible service exception that must be documented, from admin assets that must be local
Rejects 'hotfix without releases' through remote code as a reason, since updates must come through WordPress.org releases
Flags the activation POST of site URL and admin email as tracking without consent
Recommends counting installs at the point the admin connects or registers the Tallyhub account instead
Flags installing the pro add-on zip from Tallyhub's servers from inside the plugin as banned
Allows linking to the add-on purchase page while the user installs it manually
Requires the 'Powered by' footer credit to be off by default and opt-in
Flags the '100% GDPR compliant' claim and rewrites it as helping with compliance
Requires documenting the Tallyhub service in an External services readme section

evals.prompt: Urgent: our plugin (Shipwell Labels, ~40,000 active installs on WordPress.org) has an auth bypass reported this morning. Our CTO wants to close the plugin on WordPress.org for a couple of days while we patch, then reopen it. Also yesterday's 3.4.1 release got an email saying it was 'blocked from distribution' with some findings we think are false positives. We need the fix on customer sites within the hour. How do we handle this?
evals.expected_output: Rejects temporary closure (not permitted, permanent by design, over 10,000 users needs email anyway), explains the blocked release semantics and that a new fixed release is faster than an appeal, gives the SVN tag release steps, and resets the one-hour expectation against the release cooldown.
expectations: States WordPress.org does not permit temporary closure of a plugin
Explains that author-requested closure is meant to be permanent and reopening requires a full current standards and security review
Notes a plugin above 10,000 users cannot be closed by the author from the Advanced tab and needs an email to the Plugins Team
Recommends shipping the fixed version as the response instead of closing
Explains that a blocked release is not offered as an update while the previous distributed version keeps being served and the plugin stays open
Recommends fixing the findings and shipping a new version rather than waiting on a false-positive appeal
Says a false-positive reply to the block email is possible but slower
Resets the one-hour target: every release waits a cooldown (about 6 hours) during an automated security review before distribution
Gives the release mechanics: bump Version, update Stable tag, commit trunk and copy to a new tag
Mentions that the new release goes through the same automated review and could be blocked again
Marks the cooldown duration as a figure to verify

evals.prompt: Our WordPress plugin (Pipeworks CRM Sync, 3 years on wordpress.org, ~2k installs) sits on page 4 for 'crm'. Readme: Tested up to 6.2, 18 tags including 'hubspot' and 'salesforce' (competitors), last code release 14 months ago, 60% of forum threads unanswered because support@ goes into our helpdesk which auto-replies. Our growth lead suggests: commit to SVN daily so we look fresh, give a 20% discount to anyone who leaves a 5-star review, and answer paid-plan billing questions in the wp.org forum since that's where people ask. What should we actually do?
evals.expected_output: Ranks fixes by effort-to-effect using the platform's open search code (name/slug match, recency decay, tested-up-to, resolved threads, rating, installs), rejects daily commits and incentivized reviews, moves paid support off the forum with the Commercial label, and fixes the auto-reply contact risk.
expectations: Says only the first five tags are displayed and used for search
Says competitor names such as hubspot or salesforce must not be used as tags
Recommends updating Tested up to, noting a readme-only change needs no new version unless release confirmation froze the tag
Explains that search scoring decays with time since last update (roughly after six months) and with a stale Tested up to
Recommends resolving forum threads because the percentage of resolved support threads feeds ranking
Labels the ranking factors as coming from the platform's own open-source search code
Rejects daily SVN commits as gaming recency against the frequent-commit guideline
Rejects discounts for 5-star reviews as compensating for reviews, a guideline violation that can close plugins
Moves paid-plan billing support off the WordPress.org forums to the vendor's own channel
Mentions opting into the Commercial label by email to get a support URL on the listing
Flags the auto-replying helpdesk contact email as not permitted and a risk to every plugin the account owns
Says a head term like crm is dominated by high-install plugins and recommends targeting long-tail integration phrases instead
Flags 18 tags as over the Guideline 12 spam limit of 12, not merely ignored

evals.prompt: Got our first review email for 'Acme Inventory Sync': 1) 'Undocumented use of a 3rd party / external service', 2) 'Generic function/class/define/namespace/option names' (we prefix with ai_), 3) inline <script> tags in the admin page. Our readme is in German because our customers are in DACH. My dev wants to fix it and submit a fresh zip as a new submission to restart cleanly. Can you write what we send back?
evals.expected_output: Keeps the existing review thread (upload the fix on the submission page, reply to the email), writes the External services block, a 4+ character prefix rename, enqueue-based script fix, English readme, and a reply that answers each point.
expectations: Advises against a new submission and to reply in the existing review email thread
Says to upload the fixed zip on the existing submission page before replying
Writes an External services section naming the Acme API host, data sent, when it is sent, and terms and privacy links
States the disclosure is required even though the external service is the vendor's own
Replaces the ai_ prefix with a distinct prefix of at least four characters applied to functions, classes, options, hooks and constants
Replaces inline script tags with wp_enqueue_script or wp_add_inline_script
Requires the readme to be written in English, with translations through translate.wordpress.org
Drafts a reply that answers each reviewer point by number
Recommends fixing every point in one upload rather than partial rounds
Mentions that a review still incomplete after about three months is rejected and can be continued by resubmitting and replying in the old thread
